claims.text: Reducing the cooling rate after rapid heating increases residence time in the liquid-to-solid transition regime.
A slower cooling rate enhances atomic diffusion during solidification.
Enhanced diffusion produces more uniform nucleation and growth of a single-phase solid solution.
Slower cooling allows elemental mixing and atomic rearrangement toward equilibrium.
The additional rearrangement associated with slower cooling suppresses premature nucleation, compositional fluctuations, phase separation, and elemental segregation.
Flash or ultrafast heating and cooling can be used to synthesize multielement HEA nanoparticles from molten droplets.
Nanoparticle thermal history can be altered through processing conditions in plasma or related high-energy synthesis regimes.
The proposed controlled intervention changes only the cooling rate while keeping composition and the rapid-heating stage constant.
Moderately slower cooling will produce a more uniform elemental distribution than the rapid-quench baseline.
Moderately slower cooling will produce a more consistent single-phase crystallographic structure than the rapid-quench baseline.
The selected single phase may be a uniformly ordered FCC phase.
Moderately slower cooling may modestly increase grain size because of extended diffusion.
Ultra-rapid cooling often kinetically traps inhomogeneous grain sizes, elemental segregation, or multiphase structures.
Rapid cooling can hinder phase separation and favor homogeneous elemental distributions in multielement alloys.
Even when cooling is fast enough to prevent gross phase separation, it may still cause detrimental kinetic trapping.
Excessively slow cooling can cause grain coarsening or unwanted equilibrium-phase formation.
There is a narrow cooling-rate window in which diffusion improves homogeneity without causing deleterious coarsening or equilibrium phase formation.
The optimal cooling-rate threshold depends on elemental composition and synthesis setup.
The proposed scope is noble-metal HEA nanoparticles containing five or more elements.
Failure of slower cooling to improve both elemental homogeneity and single-phase crystallinity, or observation of increased separation, segregation, or coarsening, would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The baseline says ultra-rapid cooling often causes segregation or multiphase structures, whereas the boundary states that sufficiently fast cooling prevents gross phase separation. These could describe different cooling-rate windows, but the hypothesis does not clearly distinguish them.
